transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-11-30
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~72 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (CTO, Sapphire), Liam O'Connor (Lead ML Eng), Raj Patel (Infra Eng)

Summary:
Redwood SE walked through KV cache architecture, eviction heuristics, and paging behavior for long-context workloads. Discussed observed cache eviction patterns from Sapphire's traces, prefix reuse, and mitigation strategies (pinning, prefetch, eviction thresholds, local NVMe paging). Agreement to run a profiled benchmark and share config playbook.

Topics Covered:
- KV cache fundamentals (per-GPU local cache, shard layout)
- Eviction heuristics and LRU-like behaviors
- Paging to host/NVMe and page-in latency impact on p95/p99
- Prefix reuse across sessions and fingerprinting techniques
- Batching and quantization interactions with KV memory usage
- VPC/on-prem deployment considerations for disk-backed paging and KMS

Transcript Body:
[14:00:05] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um today we wanted to do a focused deep dive on the KV cache stuff because you guys reported those eviction spikes during your long-context experiments.
[14:00:18] Priya: Yeah thanks, appreciate it. The pattern is like we train or fine-tune locally, then when we run long chat sessions the model seems to evict prefixes aggressively and we get tail latency spikes, sometimes timeouts.
[14:00:27] Diego: Yeah okay that matches the traces you sent. Quick TL;DR — Redwood's runtime keeps a per-GPU KV cache for attention keys/values, sharded by tensor layout. Eviction is basically recency-weighted with some heuristics for persistence if prefix reuse is detected. But if memory pressure crosses threshold it will start paging.
[14:00:45] Liam: When you say "paging" is that to host RAM or to NVMe? We saw io waits in the infra logs.
[14:00:52] Diego: Good question. For hosted/Dedicated we prefer local GPU DRAM for active kv, then ephemeral host RAM as a second tier and NVMe as third. In Private we can configure NVMe mount for persistent page store. Those page-in ops are the ones that cause the p99 spikes, because a 4-8ms page-in becomes 40-200ms depending on the IO path and concurrency.
[14:01:18] Raj: Our environment is Private VPC — so everything is on-prem-ish via cloud region with custom NVMe config. We did see page-in 120ms to 300ms during heavy concurrency.
[14:01:27] Diego: Right, and that latency ballooning compounds with batching — when a batch contains a request that misses local cache and triggers a page-in, the whole batch waits.
[14:01:37] Maya: So let's walk through the traces Liam uploaded. Diego, can you call out the eviction spikes?
[14:01:44] Diego: Sure. (screen share) In the trace we see an eviction storm at t=02:13:20 where eviction_rate jumps from ~2%/s to 15%/s across GPUs. At the same time, cache_size utilization hits 93% and we see multiple concurrent large contexts being active. The key thing is prefix churn — many sessions introduce new prefixes that are semantically similar but different tokenization, so the runtime can't reuse and treats them as unique entries.
[14:02:08] Liam: Ugh yeah that's our tokenizer variations — we have some pieces that come from legacy pipelines. Is there a fingerprinting approach we can use so similar prefixes map to the same cache key?
[14:02:18] Diego: We do a simple token-sequence hash today. For your use-case, we suggested a relaxed fingerprint: normalize punctuation + collapse whitespace + optionally apply a short lossy hashing scheme at the sentence level. That increases prefix reuse at the cost of possible false positives — but in practice we saw reuse go up 20-30% in the benchmarks.
[14:02:42] Priya: Any risk of incorrect responses if two distinct prompts hash-collide?
[14:02:47] Diego: Very low with a 64-bit hash and the normalization heuristics; but it's an operational tradeoff. We can scope a canary with your dev traffic first.
[14:02:55] Raj: Back to paging — what about using a larger host RAM tier to avoid NVMe? Our machines have extra host RAM we can dedicate.
[14:03:02] Diego: That helps. Host RAM page-in tends to be 5-20ms vs NVMe 50-200ms. If you can allocate more host RAM or set higher in-memory watermarks we can reduce page-outs. Also increasing per-GPU cache quota for high-reuse tenants is effective.
[14:03:17] Liam: How do we set per-tenant quotas? We run multiple tenants on the same node.
[14:03:22] Maya: With Redwood Dedicated/Private you can set pool-level reservations and per-model pins. We can show an example config.
[14:03:28] Diego: Also there's an adaptive eviction threshold we can tune. Instead of evicting when usage > X, we use a margin that considers upcoming request sizes — we look at 1-minute predicted allocation and delay eviction if predicted reuse is high. That reduces oscillation.
[14:03:45] Priya: That predictive piece sounds interesting. Is that part of the default runtime or opt-in?
[14:03:50] Diego: Opt-in today, but easy to enable for your tenancy. We'll provide the exact config keys.
[14:03:56] Liam: What about quantization? We ran int8 and saw more cache entries per GB but sometimes quality dipped. Does quantization change eviction behavior?
[14:04:05] Diego: Yes — quantized KV occupies less memory, so it improves effective cache capacity. However quantization affects kernel selection and sometimes changes tokenization length slightly if you also use model compilers. The main thing is that with quantization you can store more keys in DRAM, which reduces eviction frequency. But you should validate Q8 quality for your prompts — Redwood Optimize has evaluation harness for that.
[14:04:28] Priya: Could we run a hybrid: keep critical prefixes unquantized/pinned and quantize the rest?
[14:04:33] Diego: Absolutely. We support per-key or per-prefix pinning plus mix-and-match quant profiles per model. Pin the high-value prefixes into a reserved DRAM pool.
[14:04:42] Raj: For Private deployments, are there any KMS/crypto impacts if we persist pages to NVMe? Our security team wants encrypted paging.
[14:04:49] Maya: We support encrypted NVMe volumes and integrate with customer KMS/HSM. Paging files are stored on encrypted volumes and access is via the runtime process; audit logs are generated for page-in/out ops.
[14:04:58] Raj: Great. We'll need the compliance docs.
[14:05:01] Maya: We'll attach the security whitepaper and a sample NVMe encryption guide.
[14:05:05] Liam: Back to prefix reuse — is there a way to proactively warm the cache for expected prefixes?
[14:05:10] Diego: Yes, warm-up prefetching is supported. You can schedule a job that scans your recent traffic and prefetches top-N prefixes into the KV on cold start or pre-rollout. We also offer an API endpoint to bulk-populate caches. In your traces, the top 300 prefixes account for ~55% of tokens — warming those would reduce initial tail latency.
[14:05:29] Priya: The trace showed lots of small sessions with overlapping prefixes. Could session affinity help?
[14:05:34] Diego: Yes, sticky routing per-user session to the same GPU node improves reuse dramatically but at the cost of potential load imbalance. We can do soft-affinity: prefer same node but fallback allowed.
[14:05:45] Liam: Any guidance on batching so we don't amplify page-in latency?
[14:05:50] Diego: Keep batch sizes small for latency-sensitive endpoints. Also set a per-request "max-wait-ms" in the client so a batch won't wait too long for stragglers. For throughput jobs we can use large batches and prefetch keys. Redwood Runtime also supports speculative execution where one replica proceeds without waiting for a slow page-in and the other continues when page-in completes — it's a more advanced fallback pattern.
[14:06:12] Priya: Hmm speculative exec sounds safe? Risk of duplicated responses?
[14:06:17] Diego: There's a cost tradeoff but it's deterministic; we dedupe and ensure log correlation.
[14:06:23] Raj: Are there metrics we should capture to diagnose further?
[14:06:26] Diego: Yes capture these: cache_hit_rate (per-prefix and per-model), eviction_rate, avg_evicted_duration (how old entries are when evicted), pagein_latency_p50/p95/p99, io_wait, gpu_memory_utilization, batch_tail_wait_time. If you can annotate traces with request-id we can map tail latencies to specific page-in events.
[14:06:46] Liam: We'll add those to our exporter.
[14:06:49] Priya: You mentioned prefix fingerprinting earlier — any sample code?
[14:06:53] Diego: We'll include a snippet in the playbook: normalize -> remove stop tokens -> collapse whitespace -> hash64. Also include an optional semantic fingerprint using a small embedding + locality-sensitive hash for fuzzy matches, but that's heavier.
[14:07:09] Maya: Ok quick recap of recommended mitigations for your environment: 1) increase host RAM reservation and bump DRAM watermarks, 2) enable relaxed prefix fingerprinting to improve reuse, 3) pin top prefixes into a reserved pool, 4) run warm-up prefetch job during cold starts, 5) tune batch size and client max-wait, 6) run profiled benchmark with page-in tracing.
[14:07:29] Priya: Sounds good. Can you include concrete numbers for the watermarks and thresholds?
[14:07:33] Diego: Yes in the playbook we'll add example settings — e.g., set eviction_start_threshold=85%, eviction_aggressive_threshold=95%, reserve_pool=8% of GPU DRAM for pinned prefixes, host_ram_margin=20% of total host RAM before NVMe used. Those are starting points, we should tune them in the benchmark.
[14:07:55] Liam: For the benchmarking, what do you need from our side?
[14:07:58] Diego: The anonymized traces, representative concurrency matrix (qps and burst patterns), and the list of critical prefixes you want pinned. Also indicate which models and quantization profiles you're testing.
[14:08:08] Raj: We'll produce that.
[14:08:10] Maya: I'll create a benchmark plan template and Diego will add profiling steps.
[14:08:14] Priya: Any concerns about multi-tenant interference if we pin prefixes?
[14:08:18] Diego: Pinning reduces available cache for others, so for multi-tenant setups we recommend reservation at pool-level or set tenant-level caps. We'll include a sample pool config to avoid noisy-neighbor evictions.
[14:08:29] Liam: Also, we saw noise from background eval jobs. Should we isolate evals to separate pools?
[14:08:34] Diego: Yes, isolate non-prod workloads to separate pools or schedule them during low traffic windows.
[14:08:39] Priya: Anything else on encryption/compliance?
[14:08:42] Maya: We'll attach the NVMe encryption guide, SOC2 artifacts, and config snippets for audit logging of page operations.
[14:08:50] Raj: Great. Timeline — can we aim to run the first benchmark next week?
[14:08:54] Maya: Yes, Diego and I can be on the call. We'll propose slots in the follow-up invite.
[14:08:59] (brief cross-talk, scheduling)
[14:09:12] Liam: One practical question — should we increase batch_size to improve throughput even if we get occasional p99s?
[14:09:18] Diego: Depends on SLA. For interactive features keep latency-first. For batch generation (reports, offline jobs) increase batch_size. We can do mixed policies per-route via the Redwood routing layer.
[14:09:30] Priya: Ok that's helpful.
[14:09:34] Maya: Alright last thing — any competitors you guys are evaluating?
[14:09:38] Priya: We're also running a PoC with RampantAI but they don't have good private NVMe paging support; CloudEndpt is strong on autoscaling but less observability.
[14:09:48] Maya: Noted. We'll emphasize our observability and policy controls in the follow-up.
[14:09:53] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[14:09:55] Maya: Thanks, we'll share the playbook and benchmark template after the call.
[14:10:00] (meeting continues with short scheduling and wrap-up chatter)
